strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: user-level private federated speech recognition with large models, heterogeneous speaker data, and domain mismatch between public pretraining and federated adaptation.

The empirical benefit of per-layer clipping is substantial. In Table 1, at the same clipping budget and simulated noise level, dimension-based per-layer clipping improves English test WER from 31.1% to 20.4%. This is a useful insight from revisiting established techniques.

The experimental investigation is extensive, covering initialization, cohort size, data heterogeneity, optimizers, augmentation, local computation, and three languages. Transferring training configurations across languages provides useful evidence of robustness.

The appendices document architecture, preprocessing, hyperparameters, and computational costs. Public datasets, disjoint speaker splits, and an explicit public-seed assumption are appropriate for the experimental scope. The population extrapolation and deployment limitations are openly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The advertised convergence rate is not established. Corollary 1 requires κ = 1 − 8(1 − η_loc T_loc)^2 > 0, but its prescribed η_loc = Θ(1/(L√(T_loc T))) makes κ approach −7 as T increases with fixed T_loc. Thus the asymptotic argument violates its own assumptions. Furthermore, the nonvanishing DP-noise term does not establish convergence to a stationary point at fixed noise.

The proof has additional substantive gaps. Equations (33)–(34), and the corresponding sampled-client analysis, treat the LAMB preconditioner as independent of DP noise, although it is computed from the current noisy update. The factorization and removal of cross terms therefore require correction. Equation (20) also invokes bounded gradients as a consequence of smoothness, which does not follow on the stated unbounded parameter domain. These issues undermine a central claimed contribution.

The headline privacy–utility results remain unvalidated extrapolations. The principal English experiments use 34,753 users and cohorts of 1,024, with reported privacy bounds far above useful levels. The ε = 4.5 and 7.2 claims pair measured WERs with hypothetical populations of approximately 7 million and 70 million users and cohorts of 204,800. Nonprivate scaling experiments up to 5,120 clients provide some supporting evidence, but do not establish unchanged utility under this much larger joint scaling. A validated scaling analysis or useful-privacy result at an evaluated scale is needed.

The privacy accountant is not adequately connected to the implemented mechanism. Theorem 1 assumes independent Bernoulli sampling, whereas Algorithm 1 explicitly fixes cohort size in practice. These sampling schemes require compatible sensitivity and accounting analyses. Additionally, under Bernoulli sampling, the aggregate per-client noise has cohort-dependent variance; its equivalence to fixed-variance server Gaussian noise in Appendix I.1 is not automatic.

The claimed necessity and generality of combining LAMB with per-layer clipping are insufficiently isolated. The optimizer comparisons in Tables 8–9 concern nonprivate FL; a controlled optimizer-by-clipping comparison under DP is missing. Only one model size and architecture are studied, limiting conclusions about depth-driven heterogeneity and applicability beyond ASR. Per-layer improvements are also much smaller for French and German.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement despite the extensive documentation. Code release is only promised, and WER results lack independent-run variability estimates. Table 1 reports inconsistent ε values for identical accountant inputs: z = 1.024, q = 0.0295, and T = 2,006 yield both approximately 1.3 and 13. Corrected accounting scripts and uncertainty estimates would materially strengthen confidence in the benchmark.
